abstract: A K-band frequency tripler with high harmonic 1 rejection and a wide operating bandwidth is presented. 2 The tripler design uses a triple-push topology, where three 3 phase-shifted replicas of the input signal are coherently com4 bined to suppress the fundamental and undesired harmonics, 5 thereby alleviating the tradeoff between harmonic rejection and 6 bandwidth in conventional triplers. A passive all-pass filter is 7 analyzed in detail and optimized to generate accurate 120◦spaced 8 signals for robust harmonic suppression over a wide bandwidth. 9 These signals drive three class-C–biased differential pairs whose 10 outputs are combined to generate the desired third-harmonic 11 signal. A low-Q resonant network tuned at the third harmonic 12 is incorporated at the output to enable wideband operation. 13 A highly linear buffer is also employed to increase the output 14 power level and isolate the tripler core from load variations. 15 Fabricated in a 22-nm FDSOI CMOS process, the tripler achieves 16 a 32% fractional bandwidth from 21 to 29 GHz. Measurements 17 show output power > −1 dBm across the band, with a peak of 18 +2.5 dBm at 25 GHz while consuming 25 mW. The unwanted 19 harmonics are suppressed by >37 dBc, with the fundamental 20 attenuated by >40 dBc across the frequency range. The results 21 demonstrate a power-efficient and broadband solution for high22 purity K-band frequency generation, with application areas in 23 wideband mm-wave systems. 24

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
paragraphs: 28 T HE demand for high data rates, improved sensing capabil- 29 ities, and compact wireless systems has driven interest in 30 circuits operating at millimeter-wave (mm-wave) frequencies. 31 The mm-wave spectrum offers large contiguous bandwidth that 32 can support multi-gigabit data rates. Within this spectrum, 33 the K-band (20–30 GHz) is notably attractive due to its 34 relatively low propagation loss compared to the higher mm- 35 wave bands. In particular, this range is widely used in satellite 36 communications, short-range radar systems, 5G networks, and 37 AQ:1 Received 29 May 2026; revised 3 August 2026 and 2 September 2026; accepted 23 September 2026. The VCO must 42 satisfy demanding specifications, particularly low phase noise 43 (PN) and wide frequency tuning range (FTR) [6]. To achieve 44 a multi-GHz FTR, varactors with a large capacitance tuning 45 range are incorporated within the VCO; however, their low 46 quality factor at mm-wave frequencies adversely impacts PN. 47 This poses a tradeoff between PN and wide FTR. 48 To mitigate these limitations, a common approach is to 49 generate the signal at a lower frequency, where the VCO 50 design is more robust, and then translate it to mm-wave fre- 51 quencies using a frequency multiplier. This enables the VCO 52 to operate with lower power consumption and reduced PN [5], 53 [7], [8]. Consequently, broadband multipliers become essential 54 building blocks in such architectures. In addition, preserving 55 the spectral purity of the multiplier output is critical to avoid 56 spurious harmonic components that could corrupt transmit- 57 ted/received signals [9] or degrade the blocker rejection and 58 linearity performance of the transceiver chain (as shown in 59 Fig. 1). This approach can be extended to a multiplication 60 chain to generate LO signals at E-, W-, and D-bands [10], 61 [11], [12]. In such cases, maintaining spectral purity becomes 62 even more crucial, as spurious tones can be shifted close to 63 the final LO frequency by intermodulation/mixing processes 64 within the frequency generation chain [13]. 65 2 IEEE JOURNAL OF SOLID-STATE CIRCUITS Odd-order frequency multipliers rely on device nonlinear- 66 ities to generate strong higher order harmonics, making it 67 challenging to maintain high spectral purity without sacrificing 68 bandwidth, efficiency, or output power. Waveform shaping and 69 harmonic engineering have been used to design low-spurious 70 triplers. In [14], the time-domain waveform of an overdriven 71 signal is shaped with a deep cut to increase the third-harmonic 72 content and suppress the fundamental component, but only 73 achieves a 12 dBc rejection of the first harmonic. The 74 current-folding technique proposed in [15] achieves excellent 75 harmonic rejection by folding the transconductance character- 76 istic of the MOS device three times within a single cycle to 77 synthesize a strong third-harmonic component. However, its 78 bandwidth remains limited. Another attempt [16] employed a 79 class-F technique [similar to a class-F power amplifier (PA)] 80 by adding a matching network at the output to show high 81 impedance for the third harmonic. Although high efficiency is 82 achieved, it suffers from a narrow bandwidth. 83 Another category of tripler designs relies on the self-mixing 84 technique [17], [18], [19], [20], [21], where a push–push dou- 85 bler is cascaded with a mixer to exploit the strong second-order 86 nonlinearity of MOS devices. The generated second harmonic 87 is mixed with the input to produce the third harmonic. How- 88 ever, this inherently generates both the fundamental and the 89 third-harmonic components at the output, requiring a notch 90 filter [19], [21] or feedforward cancellation [17] to suppress 91 the fundamental. Although a fundamental rejection ratio (FRR) 92 of 33 dBc has been reported, the total harmonic rejection 93 ratio (HRR) is limited by second-harmonic leakage from the 94 mixer. Harmonic injection locking has also been adopted for 95 frequency tripling [3], [22]. However, the achievable 3-dB 96 bandwidth is limited by the oscillator locking range despite 97 its demonstrated excellent spectral purity. 98 In this work, a frequency tripler for LO generation at 99 K-band is presented. The tripler achieves wide operational 100 bandwidth, high power efficiency, and outstanding HRR. The 101 tripler uses an N-push technique to improve the rejection of 102 unwanted harmonics without relying on a high-Q output filter. 103 A fully passive multi-phase generation circuit is proposed 104 to generate the phase-shifted signals required by the N-push 105 technique over a wide bandwidth. This proposed network 106 enables phase generation with zero DC power consumption, 107 thereby improving the overall efficiency of the frequency 108 multiplier. In addition, the passive phase-generation mecha- 109 nism avoids introducing additional harmonic components at 110 the tripler input, thereby preserving the phase and amplitude 111 balances essential for effective N-push operation. This article 112 is organized as follows. Section II reviews the tripler topology. 113 Section III describes the tripler architecture and its implemen- 114 tation. The measurement results are reported in Section IV 115 along with a comparison with the state-of-the-art triplers. 116 Finally, the work is concluded in Section V. 117

subsections.title: Tripler Core
paragraphs: 186 The harmonic content of a MOS device is strongly influ- 187 enced by its class of operation, which is determined by the 188 conduction angle (θc). Fig. 5(a) illustrates the short-circuit 189 drain current density of the NMOS device used in this design. 190 It can be observed that a conduction angle of θc ≈150◦, 191 corresponding to class-C operation, yields the maximum third- 192 harmonic content. Accordingly, the transistors are biased to 193 operate near this conduction angle. To account for different 194 input signal amplitudes, the bias point can be adjusted to 195 maintain the desired conduction angle [10] [as shown in 196 Fig. 5(b)]. The output current waveforms, shown in Fig. 5(c), 197 confirm operation in class-C at θc = 150◦for all signal 198 amplitudes (Asig). 199 From Fig. 5(a), it can be observed that the fundamental 200 component of the output current is approximately 15 dB higher 201 than the third-harmonic at the chosen θc. Since a practical 202 low-Q output resonator provides only 15–19 dB suppression 203 of the fundamental while maintaining a 10-GHz bandwidth [as 204 shown in Fig. 2(b)], the resulting FRR is limited to <5 dBc. 205 4 IEEE JOURNAL OF SOLID-STATE CIRCUITS Fig. 6. In contrast, by employing the triple-push topology, the FRR 206 can reach up to 20 dBc under optimum bias conditions (assum- 207 ing realistic driving signals with 0.5-dB amplitude imbalance 208 and 3◦phase imbalance), even in the absence of any filtering 209 (as shown in Fig. 6). 210 The harmonic rejection of the triple-push topology is sensi- 211 tive to phase and amplitude imbalances in the input signals and 212 rapidly degrades with increasing mismatches. Phase mismatch 213 (1φ) is the deviation from the ideal phase relationship between 214 the 0◦input and the ±120◦inputs, while α denotes the 215 amplitude ratio of the ±120◦inputs relative to the 0◦input. 216 For a reasonable α of −1.5 dB (corresponding to 0.85), the 217 allowed |1φ| must be ≤4◦to ensure a minimum fundamental 218 suppression of 15 dBc prior to filtering, as shown in Fig. 7. 219 Fig. 8(a) presents the tripler core schematic. The differ- 220 ential triple-push devices are sized at 17.28 µm/18 nm as 221 a compromise between achieving high output power (which 222 favors larger devices) and minimizing the loading effects on 223 the preceding phase-generation stage. A tail inductor (∼400 224 pH) is employed to suppress common-mode gain that arises 225 from layout asymmetries. Cascode transistors M7,8 are used to 226 improve the input–output isolation and reduce coupling that 227 disturbs the phase relationships established by the preceding 228 circuitry. In addition, the cascode arrangement improves the 229 gain by enhancing the current-to-voltage conversion [as shown 230 in Fig. 8(b)]. The tripler is loaded by a resonant tank tuned 231 at 3 fo. Small series resistors (7 ) are used to reduce the 232 tank quality factor, thus broadening the bandwidth. Post- 233 Fig. 8. An all-pass filtering approach is adopted 243 instead of conventional LPF–HPF-based phase shifters, as it 244 inherently maintains a relatively flat amplitude response while 245 providing the desired phase rotation [26]. This is achieved by 246 leveraging two LC resonant sections to produce the required 247 phases (as shown in Fig. 9). Compared to traditional RC 248 polyphase filters, the LC-based structure exhibits significantly 249 lower insertion loss and can provide voltage gain without 250 linearity constraints. Moreover, LC-based implementations 251 benefit from reduced thermal noise contributions compared 252 to their resistive counterparts. subsections.label: C.
subsections.title: Output Buffer
paragraphs: 414 To boost the output power at the generated third harmonic, 415 a buffer stage is used [as shown in Fig. 13(a)]. This stage 416 serves to isolate the phase-generation and tripler core circuitry 417 from the load, while providing additional gain. The buffer 418 adopts a pseudo-differential cascode topology. The cascode 419 configuration suppresses the Miller effect, thereby preserving 420 the high-frequency performance required at the third-harmonic 421 frequency. The pseudo-differential implementation avoids the 422 need for a tail current source, reducing voltage headroom 423 requirements. The buffer is biased in class-AB to achieve high 424 linearity and avoid creating additional harmonics. 425 The buffer is matched to the optimum load impedance 426 that maximizes power delivery at the third harmonic. This 427 is analogous to PA load-pull optimization, where the load is 428 selected to maximize output power rather than to achieve a 429 specific voltage gain or impedance match. A T-network is used 430 for wideband operation, with its component values chosen 431 to present the required impedance based on the load-pull 432 results in Fig. 13(b). The optimum differential load impedance 433 8 IEEE JOURNAL OF SOLID-STATE CIRCUITS Fig. 15. Measurement setup for evaluating the tripler. at 25 GHz is (350 + 270 j), which corresponds to an output 434 power of +6 dBm. 435 The simulated buffer S-parameters show a peak gain of 436 15 dB with a 3-dB bandwidth of 12 GHz centered at 25 GHz 437 [as shown in Fig. 13(c)]. The simulated S22 is <−6 dB across 438 the band, reflecting the tradeoff between output matching 439 and presenting the optimum load-pull impedance. Owing to 440 its bandpass response, the buffer contributes to harmonic 441 suppression by attenuating the fundamental and fifth-harmonic 442 components by up to 10 and 6 dBc, respectively. The simulated 443 OP1dB is +4.5 dBm, indicating ∼1.5 dB loss in the matching 444 network. The buffer consumes 15 mA from a 1.2 V supply. 445

sections.label: IV.
sections.title: MEASUREMENTS
paragraphs: 446 The tripler chip is implemented in the GlobalFoundries 447 22-nm FDSOI process and occupies a core area of 0.79 × 448 0.37 mm2 (as shown in Fig. 14). The chip is characterized 449 using on-chip probing with GSSG 1.85-mm probes at both 450 the input and output ports, while DC bias and supply voltages 451 are applied through DC probes. A Keysight four-port N5247A 452 PNA-X network analyzer is used to generate the input signal 453 (at fout/3) and measure the output power at different har- 454 monics, as shown in Fig. 15. Phase-matched cables are used 455 between the RF probes and the analyzer to preserve differential 456 signal balance. A calibration substrate is used to de-embed the 457 measurement setup losses up to the probe tips. 458 The measured output power at the third harmonic reaches 459 a maximum of +2.5 dBm at 25 GHz and exhibits a 460 flat response across frequency, achieving a 3-dB bandwidth 461 from 21 to 29 GHz (as shown in Fig. 16). The fundamental 462 component is suppressed at the output, remaining below 463 −40 dBm, while the fifth harmonic appears with power levels 464 between −35 and −41 dBm [as shown in Fig. 16(a)]. The resulting FRR, HRR2, HRR4, and HRR5 are 486 shown in Fig. 18, together with their corresponding mean 487 (µ) and standard deviation (σ) values. The rejection ratios 488 remain within acceptable ranges, confirming the robustness of 489 the proposed architecture. 490 The input and output matching of the tripler are < −6 dB 491 across the band (as shown in Fig. 19). The conversion loss 492 reaches a minimum of 7.5 dB at the center frequency with an 493 input power of +10 dBm [as shown in Fig. 19(b)]. The input 494 power is swept from 0 to +15 dBm, and the conversion loss is 495 measured at different frequencies (as shown in Fig. 20). The 496 best conversion loss is consistently achieved for input power 497 levels between +8 and +12 dBm across the band, where the 498 tripler core operates close to the optimum conduction angle 499 for third-harmonic generation. Beyond this point, compression 500 and harmonic redistribution degrade the conversion efficiency. 501 The harmonic purity of the output signal is also evaluated 502 for different power levels. The tripler, including the output buffer, consumes a total 511 DC power of 24–27 mW from a 1.2-V supply [as shown in 512 Fig. 22(a)]. Approximately 70% of the power is consumed 513 by the output buffer, while the remaining power is dissipated 514 in the tripler core. The measured efficiency (defined as the 515 ratio between output power at the third harmonic and con- 516 sumed DC power) reaches 7.1% near the center frequency. 517 Above 27 GHz, the efficiency decreases due to the increased 518 passive losses and the roll-off in the buffer gain. The measured 519 PN of the tripler is shown in Fig. 22(b). As expected for 520 a frequency tripler, the output PN follows the input source 521 PN with an approximately 20 log(3) (≈9.5 dB) degradation 522 due to frequency multiplication. The measured phase-noise 523 profile closely tracks that of the input source, indicating that 524 the proposed tripler introduces negligible additional PN. 525 Table I summarizes the performance of the frequency 526 tripler and compares it with previously reported state-of- 527 the-art frequency triplers. The implemented tripler achieves 528 the highest fractional bandwidth (32%) and the best overall 529 harmonic rejection performance among the reported works 530 while demonstrating a competitive peak efficiency of 7.1%. 531

sections.title: CONCLUSION
paragraphs: 532 This work presents a wideband frequency tripler with high 533 HRR implemented in 22-nm FDSOI. The triple-push topology 534 is used to enhance harmonic rejection without compromising 535 bandwidth. A novel polyphase filter is developed to generate 536 three signals with 120◦phase spacing required for proper 537 triple-push operation. Measurements demonstrate a peak out- 538 put power of +2.5 dBm with a 3-dB bandwidth spanning 539 21–29 GHz. The tripler achieves a minimum conversion 540 loss of 7.5 dB, along with state-of-the-art harmonic rejection 541 performance, including an FRR exceeding 40 dBc and an HRR 542 > 37 dBc with a peak efficiency of 7.1%.
